argument: Isaiah Berlin distinguished 'negative freedom' (freedom from interference) from 'positive freedom' (the actual ability to act on one's options), and warned that positive freedom's ambiguous link to 'self-rule' makes it easy for regimes to redefine freedom as conformity to some externally imposed standard, as Rousseau did with the 'general will.' Berlin traced this danger back to the Enlightenment's 'monism,' the assumption, borrowed from mathematics, that every question has one correct answer reachable by a single method that will cohere into one worldview, arguing this same monolithic thinking, applied to billions of different human lives, produced 20th-century totalitarianism, and proposed 'pluralism,' multiple, equally rational but conflicting ends, as an alternative to both monism and mere relativism.
keyIdeas: Negative freedom is freedom from outside interference; positive freedom requires not just the opportunity but the actual ability to act on one's options.

Berlin worried that positive freedom's link to 'self-rule' is dangerously ambiguous, since Rousseau defined self-rule as adherence to the 'general will,' letting anyone who disagreed be labeled as failing to truly self-rule.

Enlightenment thinkers borrowed three assumptions from mathematics, that a single correct answer exists, a clear method can find it, and answers cohere into one worldview, but Berlin argues none of these hold for philosophy's moral and political questions.

This 'monism,' the drive to reduce everything to one master value or answer, runs throughout Western thought and, applied to political life, leads to the totalitarian certainty behind movements like Marxism and National Socialism.

Berlin distinguishes pluralism from relativism: relativism says differing preferences have nothing more to say for them, while pluralism holds that different, even conflicting, ends can each be arrived at by fully rational people.

terms.def: Freedom from interference or obstruction by outside entities.
The actual ability, not just the opportunity, to act on one's options; sometimes clarified by Berlin as 'self-rule.'
The assumption that there is one single correct answer to every question, reachable by one method, cohering into one worldview.
The view that there are many different, sometimes conflicting, ends that people can arrive at while remaining fully rational, distinct from relativism.
Thinkers who opposed Enlightenment universalism, individualism, and industrial modernity, favoring particulars, community, and romantic nature.
